Insurance

TipHow these exercises work

Each topic starts with a real scenario and a bar model, then three levels of exercises. Level 1 (Guided) fills in the blanks of a finished function. Level 2 (Practice) applies it to new numbers. Level 3 (Challenge) asks a new question with little scaffolding. The R and Python exercises run in your browser: click Run Code to try, Submit Answer to check, and use the hint or solution if you get stuck. Excel exercises have a solution you can reveal.

Book Topics

  • The rule: insure losses you can’t absorb; cover small ones from your emergency fund (leave room for error)
  • Insurance words: premium, deductible, claim, coverage limit, liability; premiums and deductibles move in opposite directions
  • Health insurance: never go without; stay on a parent’s plan until 26, get it through work, or use the marketplace; copay, coinsurance, and the out of pocket maximum (your worst case, capped at $10,600 in 2026); high deductible plans qualify for an HSA with a deductible of at least $1,700 and an out of pocket maximum of no more than $8,500
  • Auto insurance: liability of at least 100/300/100; consider dropping collision and comprehensive on a cheap car
  • Renters insurance: about $13 to $23 a month; choose replacement cost over actual cash value
  • Disability insurance: about 1 in 4 of today’s 20 year olds will become disabled before retirement age; take employer long term disability (about 60% of pay)
  • Life insurance: only if someone depends on your income; buy term, about 10 times yearly income; skip whole life
  • Umbrella insurance: $1 million or more of extra liability; revisit as net worth grows
  • What to skip: extended warranties, phone insurance, life insurance with no dependents, single event policies

Choosing a Deductible

A higher deductible lowers your premium but costs more on each claim. The break even point is how many years of premium savings it takes to cover the extra deductible.

Formula: Break even years = (Higher deductible − Lower deductible) ÷ Yearly premium savings

Car insurance costs $1,500 a year with a $500 deductible, or $1,350 with a $1,000 deductible. ($1,000 − $500) ÷ $150 = about 3.3 years. If you file a claim less often than that, the higher deductible comes out ahead.

How to read this result: a positive yearly gain means the higher deductible saves money on average. The gain turns negative only if you claim more often than the break even. Either way, pick the higher deductible only if your emergency fund can cover it.

Level 1: Guided

Fill in the blanks to finish break_even_years(), then find how many claim-free years it takes for a $1,000 deductible (instead of $500) that saves $150 a year to pay off.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put the higher deductible in A2 (1000), the lower one in B2 (500), and the yearly savings in C2 (150). Find the break-even years in D2.

NoteSolution 
=(A2 - B2) / C2

This returns 3.3 years.

#| exercise: deduct_1_py
def break_even_years(high_deductible, low_deductible, yearly_savings):
    return (______ - ______) / yearly_savings

break_even_years(1000, 500, 150)

The extra risk you take on is the difference between the two deductibles.

Solution. 

def break_even_years(high_deductible, low_deductible, yearly_savings):
    return (high_deductible - low_deductible) / yearly_savings

break_even_years(1000, 500, 150)
#| exercise: deduct_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 3.333333) < 0.0001:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: about 3.3 years without a claim."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Subtract the lower deductible from the higher one."}
feedback
#| exercise: deduct_1_r
break_even_years <- function(high_deductible, low_deductible, yearly_savings) {
  (______ - ______) / yearly_savings
}
break_even_years(1000, 500, 150)

The extra risk you take on is the difference between the two deductibles.

Solution. 

break_even_years <- function(high_deductible, low_deductible, yearly_savings) {
  (high_deductible - low_deductible) / yearly_savings
}
break_even_years(1000, 500, 150)
#| exercise: deduct_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(abs(as.numeric(.result) - 3.333333) < 0.0001)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: about 3.3 years without a claim.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Subtract the lower deductible from the higher one.")
}

Level 3: Challenge

Back to the $1,000 vs. $500 choice that saves $150 a year. If you file one claim every k years, your yearly gain from the higher deductible is 150 − 500 ÷ k. Of k = 2, 3, 5, and 10, what is the most frequent claim rate (smallest k) where the higher deductible comes out ahead?

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put k in A2:A5, the yearly gain in B, and find the smallest k with a positive gain.

NoteSolution

In B2, filled down: =150 - 500/A2. Then:

=MINIFS(A2:A5, B2:B5, ">0")

The answer is 5. Claiming every 2 or 3 years, the lower deductible is cheaper.

#| exercise: deduct_3_py
claim_every = [2, 3, 5, 10]
# smallest k with a positive yearly gain

Use min(k for k in claim_every if 150 - 500 / k > 0).

Solution. 

claim_every = [2, 3, 5, 10]
min(k for k in claim_every if 150 - 500 / k > 0)
#| exercise: deduct_3_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 5) < 0.001:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: claiming every 5 years or less often, the higher deductible wins."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Keep the k values with a gain above zero, then take the smallest."}
feedback
#| exercise: deduct_3_r
claim_every <- c(2, 3, 5, 10)
# smallest k with a positive yearly gain

Compute gain <- 150 - 500 / claim_every for all four at once, then min(claim_every[...]).

Solution. 

claim_every <- c(2, 3, 5, 10)
gain <- 150 - 500 / claim_every
min(claim_every[gain > 0])
#| exercise: deduct_3_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(abs(as.numeric(.result) - 5) < 0.001)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: claiming every 5 years or less often, the higher deductible wins.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Keep the k values with a gain above zero, then take the smallest.")
}

Comparing Two Health Plans

A health plan’s real yearly cost is its premiums plus your share of medical bills, minus any money your employer puts in your HSA. Your share can never go above the out of pocket maximum.

Formula: Yearly cost = (Monthly premium × 12) + min(Medical bills, Out of pocket max) − Employer HSA money

This simple version assumes you pay all medical bills up to the out of pocket maximum, so it slightly overstates plans with coinsurance.

Plan A has a $100 monthly premium and a $3,000 out of pocket maximum. Plan B has a $40 monthly premium, a $5,000 out of pocket maximum, and $500 a year from your employer in the HSA. In a healthy year ($300 of care), Plan A costs $1,500 and Plan B costs $280. In the worst year, Plan A costs $4,200 and Plan B costs $4,980.

How to read this result: the gap between the lines is what you save (or lose) with Plan B. Below $4,220 of bills, Plan B wins by up to $1,220. Above it, Plan A wins by at most $780. If you put Plan B’s savings into the HSA, one healthy year covers the difference.

Level 1: Guided

Fill in the blanks to finish plan_cost(), then find Plan A’s yearly cost ($100 a month, $3,000 out-of-pocket max) in a healthy year with $300 of medical bills.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put the premium in A2 (100), bills in B2 (300), the out-of-pocket max in C2 (3000), and employer HSA money in D2 (0). Find the yearly cost in E2.

NoteSolution 
=A2*12 + MIN(B2, C2) - D2

This returns $1,500.

#| exercise: health_1_py
import numpy as np
def plan_cost(monthly_premium, medical_cost, oop_max, employer_hsa=0):
    return monthly_premium * ______ + np.minimum(medical_cost, ______) - employer_hsa

plan_cost(100, 300, 3000)

Premiums are paid every month. You never pay more in bills than the out-of-pocket max.

Solution. 

import numpy as np
def plan_cost(monthly_premium, medical_cost, oop_max, employer_hsa=0):
    return monthly_premium * 12 + np.minimum(medical_cost, oop_max) - employer_hsa

plan_cost(100, 300, 3000)
#| exercise: health_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 1500) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $1,500 in a healthy year."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. 12 months of premiums, and bills capped at oop_max."}
feedback
#| exercise: health_1_r
plan_cost <- function(monthly_premium, medical_cost, oop_max, employer_hsa = 0) {
  monthly_premium * ______ + pmin(medical_cost, ______) - employer_hsa
}
plan_cost(100, 300, 3000)

Premiums are paid every month. You never pay more in bills than the out-of-pocket max.

Solution. 

plan_cost <- function(monthly_premium, medical_cost, oop_max, employer_hsa = 0) {
  monthly_premium * 12 + pmin(medical_cost, oop_max) - employer_hsa
}
plan_cost(100, 300, 3000)
#| exercise: health_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(abs(as.numeric(.result) - 1500) < 0.01)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $1,500 in a healthy year.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. 12 months of premiums, and bills capped at oop_max.")

plan_cost(40, float("inf"), ______, employer_hsa=______)

#| exercise: health_2_py

Level 3: Challenge

Plan B is cheaper in healthy years and Plan A in bad ones. Checking medical bills from $3,000 to $5,000 in $10 steps, what is the lowest bill where Plan B costs as much as or more than Plan A?

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Work it out with algebra: above $3,000, Plan A is capped at 1,200 + 3,000, and Plan B is 480 + bills − 500.

NoteSolution

Set them equal: 480 + bills − 500 = 4,200, so =4200 - 480 + 500 gives $4,220.

#| exercise: health_3_py
#| setup: true
import numpy as np
def plan_cost(monthly_premium, medical_cost, oop_max, employer_hsa=0):
    return monthly_premium * 12 + np.minimum(medical_cost, oop_max) - employer_hsa
#| exercise: health_3_py
bills = np.arange(3000, 5001, 10)
# lowest bill where Plan B >= Plan A

plan_cost() uses np.minimum, so it works on the whole bills array. Compute a and b, then bills[b >= a].min().

Solution. 

bills = np.arange(3000, 5001, 10)
a = plan_cost(100, bills, 3000)
b = plan_cost(40, bills, 5000, employer_hsa=500)
bills[b >= a].min()
#| exercise: health_3_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 4220) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $4,220. Below that, Plan B is the cheaper bet."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Compare the two plans at every bill and keep the first where B is not cheaper."}
feedback
#| exercise: health_3_r
#| setup: true
plan_cost <- function(monthly_premium, medical_cost, oop_max, employer_hsa = 0) {
  monthly_premium * 12 + pmin(medical_cost, oop_max) - employer_hsa
}
#| exercise: health_3_r
bills <- seq(3000, 5000, by = 10)
# lowest bill where Plan B >= Plan A

plan_cost() uses pmin(), so it works on all bills at once. Compute a and b, then min(bills[b >= a]).

Solution. 

bills <- seq(3000, 5000, by = 10)
a <- plan_cost(100, bills, 3000)
b <- plan_cost(40, bills, 5000, employer_hsa = 500)
min(bills[b >= a])
#| exercise: health_3_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(abs(as.numeric(.result) - 4220) < 0.01)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $4,220. Below that, Plan B is the cheaper bet.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Compare the two plans at every bill and keep the first where B is not cheaper.")
}
